title: Understanding the Use of Images to Spread COVID-19 Misinformation on Twitter
screen_reason: Bottom-up content analysis of images shared in 2.3M COVID-19-hashtag tweets (1% Twitter Streaming sample, Mar-Jun 2020). Every image in 7,668 visual-similarity clusters (146,192 images) was screened for COVID-19 relevance (2,316 clusters / 39,367 images) and then hand-annotated against a five-type misinformation codebook, yielding 165 misinformation clusters containing 2,417 images. Those verbatim counts give an exact share of items in a sample judged misinformation against an external ground truth, i.e. CONTENT prevalence. Engagement and temporal comparisons are secondary.

estimates.country: users in more than 10 countries; top 5 are United States (45.8% of misinformation-sharing users), India, United Kingdom, Malaysia, South Africa
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-related ('informative') clustered images shared in COVID-19 hashtag tweets that were annotated as COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 2,417 misinformation images (in 165 clusters) of 39,367 images in the 2,316 informative clusters = 6.14%; at cluster level 165/2,316 = 7.1%
estimates.denominator: 39,367 images in the 2,316 image clusters judged 'informative' (i.e. containing visual cues or English/Chinese words connected to the COVID-19 pandemic), drawn from 339,952 images downloaded from 2,335,412 COVID-19-hashtag tweets in a 1% Twitter Streaming sample of 505,346,347 tweets
estimates.definition: The image falls into at least one of five hand-coded misinformation types - conspiracies on COVID-19, wrong understanding of the threat severity of COVID-19, fauxtography, wrong medical advice, other false claims - with the labels checked against fact-checking sources
estimates.misinfo_def: "we adopt the definition of misinformation proposed by Wu et al., which defines misinformation as 'informative content that contains incorrect or inaccurate information' [88], regardless of the purpose with which it was posted"
estimates.source_quote: At last, we have 165 image clusters identified as COVID-19 misinformation image clusters, containing 2,417 images posted by 2,403 users.
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.3 'Identifying COVID-19 misinformation images', pp. 108:10-108:11; Section 4 Results opening, p. 108:11
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors built a codebook by iterative thematic coding. Phase I (COVID-relevance): both independently labelled 1,000 random clusters, Cohen's kappa = 0.991, after which the FIRST AUTHOR ALONE labelled the remainder. Phase II (misinformation): both annotators inspected every image in all 2,316 informative clusters and reached consensus by deliberation on 165 misinformation clusters - no kappa is reported for this phase. Labels were checked against trustworthy fact-checking sources (AP News, WHO Mythbusters; Snopes and FactCheck.org cited for individual cases). Clustering accuracy was validated at 98.6% (105 of 7,773 clusters were false positives and were removed).
estimates.moderator_quote: "In the subsequent annotation, we will focus on the images contained in clusters only. The reason is that we are interested in understanding how misinformation images are re-shared on Twitter, and if images did not cluster together it is safe to assume that they did not become popular on Twitter. In fact, considering that our data is a uniform 1% sample of all public tweets and that our minimum cluster size is 5, we can assume that images that do not form clusters in our dataset were likely shared publicly on Twitter less than 500 times at the time when the data was collected."
estimates.notes: The paper never prints a prevalence percentage; this is an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts with the same denominator (2,417/39,367), which R8 permits. IMPORTANT denominator caveat driving denom_selection=curated: only images that formed a visual-similarity cluster of at least 5 in a 1% sample were annotated at all - roughly, only images shared publicly on Twitter about 500+ times. About 191K of the 339,952 downloaded images never clustered and were never screened, so this is a prevalence among POPULAR/re-shared images, not among all images. Images with text in languages other than English or Chinese were also excluded from being misinformation candidates.

estimates.notes: BROADER-DENOMINATOR variant of the row above: same numerator, denominator widened from COVID-related images to every clustered image appearing in COVID-19-hashtag tweets. Flagged definition_variant=true - do not pool both rows. The two denominators are exactly the kind of methodological choice that drives divergent prevalence estimates (6.1% vs 1.65% from identical data), which is why both are recorded. Confidence medium because the wider denominator contains images that could not have been labelled misinformation by construction.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Table 1 breaks the 165 misinformation clusters into five types (Conspiracies 91 clusters / 1,403 images; Wrong understanding of threat severity 10 / 294; Fauxtography 27 / 455; Wrong medical advice 41 / 605; Other false claims 23 / 478). No rows: the types are MULTI-LABEL ('a single image might belong to two or more categories'), the cluster counts sum to 192 and the image counts to 3,235, both above the 165/2,417 totals, so no exclusive shares can be derived. 2) Table 2 (country of misinformation-sharing users: US 1,282 users, 45.8%, and 1,354 tweets, 46.9%; India 9.3%; UK 5.1%; Malaysia 3.5%; South Africa 3.2%; top 5 = 66.9% of users) is the geographic COMPOSITION of misinformation sharers, not the prevalence of misinformation in any country, so it yields no country rows and does not meet R1 for CONCENTRATION (the group is a set of countries, not a top-X% of users). 3) Table 4 (political leanings of the 1,282 US misinformation-sharing users: pro-Democrat 546 = 42.6% / 586 tweets = 43.2%; pro-Republican 508 = 39.6% / 538 tweets = 39.7%; QAnon 111 = 8.7%; Neutral 118 = 9.2%; N/A 110 = 8.6%; 'QAnon theory adherents are around 21.9% of all users who are pro-Republicans') is one of the paper's headline findings, but it is a composition INSIDE the misinformation set - the share of misinformation sharers who are Republican, not the share of Republicans who shared misinformation - so it is not a prevalence and I created no subgroup rows. An adjudicator wanting party rows should note there is no denominator of all pro-Republican / pro-Democrat users anywhere in the paper. 4) Engagement results are medians, not shares (misinformation-image tweets: median 21 retweets, 51 likes; baseline 53 and 142; baseline with random images 62 and 151). 5) Temporal results are medians (raw lifespan 4.05 vs 1.62 days; normalised 0.38 vs 0.16 days; burst time 0.705 vs 0.276 hours). 6) Method QA numbers (98.6% clustering accuracy, 6,128/7,773 clusters with identical pHashes, 324 users (11.6%) with hashtags in bios, 'more than 80% of US users show a political leaning') are not misinformation prevalences.

rob.design: Observational, bottom-up content analysis. Source: the public 1% Twitter Streaming API, 505,346,347 tweets between 1 March and 16 June 2020. 103 COVID-19 hashtags (snowballed in March 2020 from #COVID, #coronavirus, #COVID19 plus the 100 most popular co-occurring hashtags) selected 2,335,412 COVID-19 tweets; 370,465 contained image URLs and 339,952 images were downloaded (78,348 from original tweets, 261,604 from retweets). Perceptual hashing (ImageHash) plus DBSCAN (Hamming threshold 6, minimum cluster size 5) grouped 148,987 images into 7,773 clusters; manual inspection removed 105 false-positive clusters, leaving 7,668 clusters / 146,192 images and an assessed clustering accuracy of 98.6%. Two-phase manual annotation: Phase I COVID-relevance (two annotators on 1,000 random clusters, Cohen's kappa = 0.991, remainder by the first author) gave 2,316 informative clusters / 39,367 images; Phase II misinformation coding against a five-type codebook by both annotators over all informative clusters, consensus by deliberation, no kappa reported, labels checked against AP News and WHO Mythbusters. Result: 165 misinformation clusters, 2,417 images, 2,403 users. Political-leaning coding of US users: 300 of 1,282 double-coded (kappa 0.890 for four categories; 0.941 for QAnon), remainder by the first author. Key threats: only clustered (i.e. widely re-shared) images were annotated; only images without text or with English/Chinese text were eligible; a 1% sample; the authors themselves call the dataset 'rather small'; hydroxychloroquine content was coded misinformation even though an FDA emergency use authorisation was live during part of the collection window.
rob.item6_quote: we adopt the definition of misinformation proposed by Wu et al., which defines misinformation as "informative content that contains incorrect or inaccurate information" [88], regardless of the purpose with which it was posted.
